extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students studying real analysis (sequences and series)
extracted.subtask_description: Exercises, definitions, and standard convergence tests for sequences and series of real numbers (Cauchy property, lim sup/lim inf, convergence tests such as comparison, ratio, root, alternating, p-series, absolute convergence, rearrangements). Intended to guide proofs and problem solving in a first course in real analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Cauchy sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence (x_n)_{n=1}^∞ is a Cauchy sequence if for every ε > 0 there exists M ∈ ℕ such that for all n, k ≥ M we have |x_n - x_k| < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informally: terms are eventually all arbitrarily close to each other. Use this definition directly to prove examples are/are not Cauchy (examples provided in text). The definition is the basis of the Cauchy criterion for convergence in complete metric spaces like ℝ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: Cauchy implies bounded
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sequence is Cauchy then it is bounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the Cauchy property to pick M with |x_n - x_M| < 1 for n ≥ M and then bounds finitely many initial terms. Useful as a quick necessary condition when checking Cauchy property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem: completeness of ℝ (Cauchy iff convergent)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of real numbers is Cauchy if and only if it converges (i.e., ℝ is Cauchy-complete).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: one direction is trivial (convergent implies Cauchy). For the other, use boundedness, lim inf/lim sup and subsequences (Bolzano–Weierstrass arguments) to show lim inf = lim sup, hence convergence. This theorem can be used as a definition of completeness in abstract settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: convergence of a series (partial sums)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a sequence (x_n), the formal series Σ_{n=1}^∞ x_n converges if its sequence of partial sums s_k = Σ_{n=1}^k x_n converges; the value of the series is lim_{k→∞} s_k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful: the symbol Σ can refer to the formal object or to the limit of partial sums depending on context. Partial sums are the primary object to examine when testing convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: tail equivalence for series
rubrics_metrics.description: Let Σ_{n=1}^∞ x_n be a series and M ∈ ℕ. Then Σ_{n=1}^∞ x_n converges if and only if Σ_{n=M}^∞ x_n converges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: partial sums differ by a fixed finite number (the initial finite sum). This justifies focusing on tails when proving convergence/divergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition / Criterion: Cauchy series
rubrics_metrics.description: A series Σ x_n is Cauchy (a Cauchy series) if the sequence of its partial sums is a Cauchy sequence. Equivalently, for every ε>0 there exists M such that for all k>n≥M, |Σ_{i=n}^k x_i| < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Series converges iff it is Cauchy. The Cauchy formulation is often used to check convergence without knowing the limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary condition: terms must tend to zero
rubrics_metrics.description: If Σ_{n=1}^∞ x_n converges then lim_{n→∞} x_n = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: from Cauchy property of partial sums take k=n+1 and let n→∞. This is a quick necessary test—if terms do not go to zero the series diverges (used for simple divergence checks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: linearity of series
rubrics_metrics.description: If Σ x_n and Σ y_n converge (real series) and α ∈ ℝ, then Σ α x_n converges to α Σ x_n, and Σ (x_n + y_n) converges to Σ x_n + Σ y_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: apply linearity to partial sums. Useful when combining/constraining series via algebraic manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: monotone nonnegative term series (monotone convergence)
rubrics_metrics.description: If x_n ≥ 0 for all n, then Σ x_n converges iff the sequence of partial sums is bounded above (equivalently: monotone increasing bounded sequence converges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since partial sums are monotone increasing, one only needs to check boundedness. The supremum gives the limit when it exists. This underpins many comparison arguments for positive-term series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: absolute convergence and conditional convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: A series Σ x_n converges absolutely if Σ |x_n| converges. If Σ x_n converges but Σ |x_n| does not, the series converges conditionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute convergence is a stronger property and confers many extra tools (rearrangements, multiplication). Proposition: absolute convergence implies convergence (proof via Cauchy criterion and triangle inequality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: comparison test
rubrics_metrics.description: Let 0 ≤ x_n ≤ y_n for all n. (i) If Σ y_n converges then Σ x_n converges. (ii) If Σ x_n diverges then Σ y_n diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: compare monotone increasing partial sums. This test is fundamental; used to compare unknown series to known benchmark series (e.g., p-series, geometric series).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: p-series test
rubrics_metrics.description: For p ∈ ℝ, the series Σ_{n=1}^∞ 1/n^p converges iff p > 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses comparison to grouped partial sums (generalization of harmonic series grouping). Use as benchmark: harmonic series (p=1) diverges; p>1 converges by bounding grouped blocks by geometric-like sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: geometric series convergence formula
rubrics_metrics.description: If |r| < 1 then the geometric series Σ_{n=0}^∞ r^n converges and Σ_{n=0}^∞ r^n = 1/(1 - r).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by explicit formula for finite sum and taking limit. Geometric series is a canonical example and a frequent comparator in ratio/root test arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: ratio test
rubrics_metrics.description: Let (x_n) be a sequence with x_n ≠ 0. If L = lim_{n→∞} |x_{n+1}/x_n| exists then (i) if L < 1 the series Σ x_n converges absolutely; (ii) if L > 1 the series Σ x_n diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: compare tail to a geometric series with ratio r where L < r < 1. Exercise notes a stronger form using lim sup. Use with caution when L = 1 (inconclusive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: root test
rubrics_metrics.description: Let L = lim sup_{n→∞} |x_n|^{1/n}. If L < 1 then Σ x_n converges absolutely; if L > 1 then Σ x_n diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof mirrors ratio test: compare |x_n| to r^n for some r with L < r < 1. Root test is useful when terms involve nth powers or factorials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: alternating series test (Leibniz criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let (x_n) be a monotone decreasing sequence of positive reals with lim_{n→∞} x_n = 0. Then the alternating series Σ_{n=1}^∞ (-1)^{n} x_n converges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses bounding of even/odd partial sums to show monotone bounded subsequences and estimates the error by the next term. Also note there exist conditionally convergent alternating series whose |x_n| go to zero arbitrarily slowly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: rearrangements preserve sum for absolutely convergent series
rubrics_metrics.description: If Σ x_n is absolutely convergent and σ: ℕ→ℕ is a bijection (a rearrangement), then Σ x_{σ(n)} is absolutely convergent and its sum equals the original sum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: absolutely convergent series may be rearranged arbitrarily without changing their sum. By contrast, conditionally convergent series can change sum under rearrangement (examples and exercises appear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy condensation principle (exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: For (x_n) a decreasing sequence of positive numbers, Σ x_n converges iff Σ 2^n x_{2^n} converges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as an exercise; widely used to test series with logarithmic factors and to decide convergence of slowly varying sequences (exercises apply it to ln n / n^2, 1/(n ln n), etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abel's theorem (exercise reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the partial sums of Σ x_n are bounded and (λ_n) is a sequence with lim_{n→∞} λ_n = 0 and some regularity (as in Abel summation hypotheses), then Σ λ_n x_n converges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text references Abel's theorem as an advanced exercise: used to transform bounded partial sums via 'summation by parts' arguments. Details are provided in the exercise statement for students to prove.
